topicTitle: Fungi: General introduction and characteristic features of phycomycetes, ascomycetes, basidiomycetes and deuteromycetes
notes: **General features.** Fungi are achlorophyllous, heterotrophic, eukaryotic organisms whose body is a thallus made of thread-like hyphae (a mycelium); cell walls contain chitin and food is stored as glycogen.
**Phycomycetes.** These lower fungi have aseptate (coenocytic) hyphae and form thick-walled zygospores sexually; examples are Mucor, Rhizopus and the plant pathogen Albugo.
**Ascomycetes.** Sac fungi have septate hyphae and produce ascospores inside sac-like asci; Saccharomyces, Aspergillus, Penicillium and morels belong to this group.
**Basidiomycetes.** Club fungi bear basidiospores on club-shaped basidia; Agaricus (button mushroom), Puccinia (wheat rust) and Ustilago (smut) are common examples.
**Deuteromycetes.** The imperfect fungi show no known sexual stage and are classified by their conidia; Alternaria, Trichoderma and Colletotrichum are important members.
Fungal walls are chitin and the reserve is glycogen, which is why a mushroom is not given a place in Plantae even when it grows in soil like a plant.

Penicillium is an ascomycete used for penicillin. Puccinia, the wheat rust, is a basidiomycete even though it never looks like a mushroom. The sexual structure decides, not the shape of the colony.
